intro: I didn't want this to be one more page of confident steps that turn out to be two years old. So the six hand-checked guides started from the providers' own docs, got checked claim by claim, and then I went and tried the setup on GitHub, Slack and Google Cloud myself. Where the docs and the rest of the internet disagreed, I went with the docs and wrote the disagreement down here. Guides the agent writes live follow the same rule, just automatically: every fact needs a quote from the page, and if the quote isn't actually there, the claim gets marked not verified.

attempts.what: Registered an OAuth app (personal account) with Composio's callback URL, 2026-10-27.
observed: The form page is titled “Register a new OAuth app”.

The callback field is now a “Redirect URIs” section with an “Add redirect URI” button and the text “You may add up to 10 redirect URIs”. GitHub's docs still call it “Authorization callback URL”, so the guide now uses the on-screen wording.
Each redirect URI has its own “Allow wildcard matching” checkbox, unticked by default.
“Expire user access tokens” was ticked by default, with the note that it provides a refresh_token.
After clicking Register: “Application created successfully”, a Client ID shown immediately, “0 users”, and a client secret generated on demand. No review or pending state.
After creation, the expiry checkbox no longer appears on the General page; the left menu has General, Optional features and Advanced.
Total time: about 3 minutes.

attempts.what: Created a fresh free workspace and a Blank app, added the redirect URL, activated public distribution, 2026-10-27.
observed: “Create New App” now opens a dialog with templates (“AI agent”, “Starter app”) and “Blank app” / “From a manifest”. The “From scratch” option named in most guides is gone.
Blank app runs a 4-step wizard (details → scopes → events → review) ending in “Create and Install”, which installs into the dev workspace immediately.
Redirect URLs accepted both the Composio https URL and a test http://example.com/callback without error. I deleted the http one.

The OAuth & Permissions page shows the live Bot User OAuth Token in plain text, plus new options: token rotation (requires a redirect URL first), PKCE opt-in, and Enterprise-Managed Authorization. I revoked the token after the screenshot exposed it.

Manage Distribution checklist: Enable Features & Functionality (ticked), Add OAuth Redirect URLs (ticked), Use HTTPS For Your Features (ticked) (all automatic), and Remove Hard Coded Information (manual confirmation).

“Activate Public Distribution” took effect instantly, with no review. The page then showed a shareable install URL and an Installation Count: 0 active workspaces in the past 28 days, updated every 24 hours.
Left menu: “Submit to Slack Marketplace” has 5 parts: App Listing, Review scopes, Security and compliance, Testing information, Automated checks.
Total time including creating the workspace: about 15 minutes.

attempts.what: Personal Google account: new project, Gmail API enabled, Google Auth Platform configured as External, Gmail scopes added. Not published. 2026-10-28.
observed: The new project sits in “No organization” (personal account), so the Audience page's “Make internal” button is disabled. External is the only option.
Data Access → “Add or remove scopes” lists only scopes for enabled APIs; Gmail scopes had to be pasted under “Manually add scopes” → Add to table → Update.
Classification shown by Google: gmail.readonly under “Your restricted scopes” (Gmail scopes); gmail.send under “Your sensitive scopes”. This confirms the send-only vs read path split in the guide.
Audience → Publishing status: “Testing”. “Publish app” is greyed out with “To publish your app, you must complete your configuration on the Branding page.”
OAuth user cap: “Allowed user cap prior to app verification is 100, and is counted over the entire lifetime of the app”, shown as a meter: 0 users (0 test, 0 other) / 100 user cap.
No billing or free-trial signup was needed for any of this.
Total time: about 20 minutes (most of it finding the right screens).

checks.claim: GitHub's form field is called “Authorization callback URL”.
checks.finding: Only found this by actually trying it: GitHub's docs still say “Authorization callback URL”, but the live form shows a “Redirect URIs” section with per-URI wildcard checkboxes. The guide uses the on-screen wording so developers don't get stuck looking for a field that isn't there.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating an OAuth app

checks.claim: Create the app with “Create New App → From scratch”.
checks.finding: Found this by trying it: the option is now “Blank app”, below new “AI agent” and “Starter app” templates, followed by a 4-step wizard that also installs the app. The guide uses the current wording.

checks.claim: gmail.readonly is restricted; gmail.send is only sensitive.
checks.finding: Confirmed in a real Cloud Console project: Google itself sorted gmail.readonly under “restricted” and gmail.send under “sensitive”. That's the difference between weeks plus a CASA audit and a few days of review.

checks.claim: The 100-user cap for unverified apps is lifetime and can't be reset.
checks.finding: The Audience page states it directly and shows a usage meter.

checks.claim: GitHub OAuth app tokens never expire, and an OAuth app has a single callback URL.
checks.finding: Out of date. Since GitHub's August 14, 2026 change, new OAuth apps issue 8-hour tokens with 6-month refresh tokens by default and accept up to 10 callback URLs. Popular libraries' docs still describe the old behaviour.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating an OAuth app

checks.claim: Any user can connect their org's repos once they authorize your OAuth app.
checks.finding: New organizations have OAuth app access restrictions on by default. Members can only request approval, and an org owner must approve. I added this as the GitHub launch gate.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: OAuth app access restrictions

checks.claim: Marketplace submission requires 5 active workspace installs.
checks.finding: A recent third-party article (Aug 2026) quotes 5. Slack's own review guide says 10 active workspaces (used in the past 28 days) and blocks submission below that. I use 10.

checks.claim: The 1-request-per-minute history limit only affects new installs of unlisted apps.
checks.finding: True when announced (May 2025), but Slack's changelog says existing installs of unlisted distributed apps moved to the new limits on March 3, 2026.
Preliminary review up to 10 business days; functional review up to 10 weeks for new apps (6 for updates). Resubmitting during the preliminary phase resets your queue position.

checks.claim: Brand verification takes 2–3 business days; sensitive scopes 3–5 business days.
checks.finding: Both figures appear on Google's own production-readiness pages.

checks.claim: Restricted-scope (Gmail read) verification takes N weeks.
checks.finding: Google publishes no fixed timeline; I only found “several weeks or longer” attributed to Google by third parties. The guide says so and marks our 42-day scoring estimate as ours.

checks.claim: CASA Tier 2 can be done with a free self-scan.
checks.finding: 2024 forum posts show Google offering a self-scan option; 2025–26 sources say a lab-verified assessment is required. The guide recommends budgeting for an authorized lab and lists this as uncertain.

checks.claim: Unlisted HubSpot apps are capped at 25 installs.
checks.finding: Confirmed for marketplace-distribution OAuth apps on the 2025.2+ platform (developer test accounts excluded), enforced since September 22, 2025.
Only found in a partner agency's write-up, which itself warns HubSpot has changed the threshold before. Marked third-party in the guide.

checks.claim: Posting on a member's behalf (w_member_social) needs partner verification.
checks.finding: A third-party guide claims so, but LinkedIn's own docs list Share on LinkedIn as a self-serve product you add in the portal. Company-page posting is the gated part.

checks.claim: Access tokens last 60 days; refresh tokens 365 days.
checks.finding: Stated in LinkedIn's docs, but the sample responses' expires_in values don't match those durations in seconds. The guide tells developers to check a live response, and notes refresh tokens are partner-only.

checks.claim: Public integrations must pass Notion's review before other workspaces can install them.
checks.finding: Review applies only to Marketplace listings (5–10 business days). A public connection works via OAuth without being listed.

checks.claim: There is one Composio callback URL.
checks.finding: Composio's docs show three: /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback (white-labeling guide), /api/v3.1/… (some preview docs) and the legacy /api/v1/auth-apps/add. Guides use v3, and tell developers to copy the exact URI from their Composio auth config.

learned: Making the app is never the hard part. It took me 3 minutes on GitHub, about 15 on Slack, about 20 on Google. What actually holds up a launch is different for every provider: a paid security audit (Google), a 25-install cap (HubSpot), throttled APIs until you're listed (Slack), partner vetting (LinkedIn), or your customer's own org admin (GitHub). So every guide leads with that, and the steps come after.

Sometimes the scope matters more than the provider. Gmail send-only is a few days of review. The moment you want to read mail it's restricted, which means weeks plus a paid audit every year. I watched Google sort the two into different buckets in the console. That's why guides have a "pick your path" bit before any steps.

A lot changed in the last year and a half. GitHub tokens expire now, Slack throttled unlisted apps, HubSpot capped installs. Blog posts and model memory lag behind all of it, so the live agent always reads today's pages and dates every source.

Composio's managed apps let you skip the approval wait while you build. The catch is that connections stick to the app they were made with, so moving users to your own app later means everyone reconnects. Every guide says this up front.
Models will happily invent a quote. So every quote gets checked against the page it supposedly came from, and anything that doesn't match is shown as not verified instead of quietly trusted.

The first real run (Zoom) looked decent on the surface: 3/5, 36 facts, 32 quotes checked out, 2 live probes. Reading it properly showed three bugs in my own agent: fact IDs leaking into sentences, Zoom's forum labelled as official, and Zoom's server-to-server docs mixed into a guide about user logins. All fixed, all tested now. The probes also turned up something I couldn't find in Zoom's docs: the sign-in page loads before Zoom checks your client ID, so a wrong ID only shows up after the user logs in.

Running Asana twice gave 3/5 and then 2/5, and one version said "Easy, same day" right next to "2 to 10 weeks". The score rules are fixed, but the facts feeding them come from a model reading docs, and Asana's docs are a bit vague about whether review is optional. I tightened what counts as a review, made the wait line agree with the score, and listed the variance below instead of pretending it isn't there.

Then I had the whole site reviewed end to end, live runs included, by a second pass that only looked for problems. It found real ones. Parsing big pages blocked the server long enough for the live page to load without its script. The Google Calendar guide probed Google Cloud's workforce sign-in instead of Google's real OAuth endpoint, because the domains were tried alphabetically. And it charged Calendar for a CASA audit and a 4 to 6 week wait from a blog, which contradicts what I'd already verified for Gmail. The fix I like most: the hand-checked guides now feed the live agent. Any Google product gets the Google facts I verified myself, and they win over anything weaker. An audit only counts if a source the agent read actually names one.

A second review pass, run against the fixed site, found what the first fixes had broken. Two live runs at once made the model client give up: every few seconds of waiting for free capacity used up one of its eight attempts. Waiting doesn't count as failing anymore, and if a run does fail it says why in plain words, offers Try again, and doesn't count against your limit. Worse, the Google Drive guide said about a week, because my sensitive-scope shortcut applied even though listing a user's files needs a restricted scope and a CASA audit. Restricted Google use cases now get weeks plus the audit, and the guide shows both paths: drive.file only (days) or reading existing files (weeks plus audit). Typing just "Google" now asks which product instead of guessing.
pipeline: Checks Composio's public toolkit page to see if there's already a managed app.
Runs four searches (creating the app, the OAuth docs, app review, verification and limits) and puts the provider's own pages first. Forums and blogs count as third-party, two at most.
Opens the pages and keeps only the paragraphs about OAuth, review, limits and timelines. Plain keyword matching, no model, which keeps it inside the free tier.
Pokes the real endpoints without logging in: the OpenID discovery file, and the actual login URL with a fake client ID, to see what error a developer would hit.
A small model pulls facts out of each page. Each fact has to come with a quote, and code checks that quote is really on the page.
If I've already verified rules for this provider family (Google, for now), those facts get added as hand-checked and win any conflict.
A bigger model writes the guide using only those numbered facts. Anything it can't back up gets marked not verified.
The score comes from the fixed rules above, not from the model.
limitations: Live guides are a good first draft, not gospel. They're only as good as what search turns up, and providers with docs behind a login come out thin.
The free Groq tier limits how fast the model can go, so a live run takes a minute or two and only two run at once.

Search runs through Tavily (free tier, roughly 200 guides a month). Without a key it falls back to DuckDuckGo, which sometimes blocks servers. You can also paste the provider's docs URL instead of the name.
Render's free plan forgets generated guides when it redeploys. The hand-checked ones live in the repo, so they always come back.
"Tested" only covers what I actually clicked through. I didn't submit anything for real review, so the review timelines come from docs, not experience.
The scoring is deliberately simple. Two apps that both score 4 can still feel very different, so read the line about what blocks launch.
Live scores can wobble between runs when a provider's docs are vague (Asana went 3/5, then 2/5). Regenerate, or check the not verified items, before trusting a live score.
To protect the free Groq and Tavily quota, each visitor can start 5 live runs per 10 minutes and the site caps at 80 a day. Asking for an app that's already being researched just shows you that run.
The restricted-scope check is Google-specific for now, because that's the provider family I verified by hand. Other providers rely on what the agent reads.
